acquisition.why: US version depends on grant pitches to churches, shelters and workforce centres, plus phone sales. The UK equivalents are relationship-heavy: Skills Bootcamps need DfE/authority procurement, and adult skills funding needs approved-provider status and employer partnerships. Paid ads for self-funded courses are possible, but the grant hook needs human partnership work.

onboarding.why: Eligibility checks, funding paperwork, ID and evidence for funded learners need human compliance review [E].

delivery.why: White-label online courses run mostly unattended. Accreditation, assessment and any hands-on or placement parts need humans.

billing.why: Funded models mean claims, audits and milestone evidence to the funder. Only self-pay course sales would be simple Stripe billing.

support.why: Learners who are sceptical or vulnerable, plus progression and job-outcome tracking for funders, need human pastoral support.

scores.R_why: The US state-grant/ETPL mechanism does not exist in the UK. UK funded training needs ESFA/DfE approved-provider status, Ofsted inspection, accredited qualifications and procurement wins. This is far beyond £300 and 6-8 h/week. Self-pay course resale without the grant is a different, weaker idea.
scores.M_why: UK funded training is a crowded, regulated provider market with large incumbents. Unfunded online certificates are commoditised and face cheap MOOCs and AI tutors.
scores.one_line: The economics rest on a US grant-reimbursement loophole with no UK equivalent within reach. For a £300 part-time agent-run test it is effectively a non-starter [E].

acquisition.why: The demonstrated scraped-mobile SMS is illegal under PECR. Lawful routes are cold email to estate-agency limited companies (many agencies are Ltd), SEO, Google Ads, and portal or app marketplaces. Agents can personalise sample-staging emails, but this is platform- and channel-dependent.

onboarding.why: Self-serve upload web app with account creation.

delivery.why: Image-model API processes photos in seconds. Spot-check quality and add mandatory 'virtually staged' labelling for UK consumer-protection and CMA/Property Ombudsman expectations.

support.why: Agents handle redo requests and FAQs. Escalate quality or misleading-image complaints.

scores.R_why: Technically easy for Ricardo, cheap to prototype and fits £300. Per-image API cost must be checked (the $3.90 claim contradicts the $1 price) [E]. UK agents already use the bundled staging from their photographers and portals.
scores.M_why: Extremely saturated (Virtual Staging AI, REimagineHome, Collov and many more). Portals and phone and photo editors are adding it natively, and generic image models let agents do it themselves.
scores.one_line: Buildable and highly automatable, but a commoditised AI wrapper with no demonstrated customers and UK misleading-listing risk. Only worth it as a quick niche test [E].

acquisition.why: YouTube audience growth is inbound, but breakout depends on creative hooks, collaborations and paid shout-outs that need the host's judgement.

onboarding.why: Booking featured local businesses and partners needs human coordination.

delivery.why: An on-camera, travelling, in-person show format needs the host physically present. Editing can be agent-assisted.

billing.why: AdSense is automatic, but sponsorship deals need negotiation.

support.why: Comment and community moderation can be largely automated.

scores.R_why: Travelling or on-location shows are incompatible with a toddler and 6-8 h/week. The source creator already had 100M monthly views, so the example is not transferable.
scores.M_why: Business-challenge and makeover content on YouTube is crowded. Monetisation is hit-driven and platform-dependent.
scores.one_line: A hit-driven, host-dependent media format that requires travel and an existing audience. It is poorly suited to an agent-run part-time UK business [E].

acquisition.why: Subscriber growth via SEO, social content, referral programmes and paid ads is inbound. Agents can draft content, but audience growth is slow and needs editorial quality.

onboarding.why: Welcome sequence plus segmentation poll in Kit, fully automated.

delivery.why: Digital products are delivered automatically. Agents can draft issues and products, with Ricardo approving the editorial voice.

billing.why: Stripe, Gumroad or Kit Commerce and affiliate networks pay automatically.

support.why: Refunds and access queries are mostly handled by agents.

scores.R_why: Cheap and fits the hours and skills, and UK GDPR consent is handled by the double opt-in. The bottleneck is building a list from zero, which typically takes many months [E]. AI-generated newsletters struggle for trust.
scores.M_why: The newsletter space is saturated and AI-generated content floods niches. Headroom exists only in specific underserved UK niches where Ricardo has credibility [E].
scores.one_line: Highly automatable stack with legal inbound acquisition, but there is no first-hand evidence and audience-building from zero is the hard, slow part [E].

acquisition.why: The described engine is partnerships, joint-venture webinars and in-person speaking events, all human. YouTube and ads are possible but secondary.

onboarding.why: 'Free strategy session' sales calls are human-led.

delivery.why: Course content can be agent-maintained. Coaching and done-for-you publishing need human or freelancer work.

support.why: Course FAQs can be automated. Author coaching questions need people.

scores.R_why: Selling publishing education needs a publishing track record and authority Ricardo lacks. The eight-figure example relies on a team, events and joint ventures. A book-led funnel for another core business is a tactic rather than a business.
scores.M_why: Self-publishing education is crowded (SelfPublishing.com, Publishing.com, Reedsy, YouTube), and AI erodes the value of writing help.
scores.one_line: An authority- and partnership-driven info business with promotional sourcing. It is hard to bootstrap without credibility and resists agent-only operation [E].

acquisition.why: Amazon search and KDP keyword discovery are inbound. Amazon Ads can be agent-managed within budget caps. This is entirely platform-dependent.

onboarding.why: No customer onboarding; Amazon handles purchase.

delivery.why: Agents can research niches and draft and format books. Amazon prints and delivers. Human quality review and KDP AI-content disclosure are still needed.

support.why: Amazon handles customer service and returns.

scores.R_why: Cheap, fits the hours, and the UK seller setup is straightforward. However, KDP limits daily title uploads and requires AI disclosure, low-quality AI books get poor reviews or are removed, and earnings for newcomers are typically small [E].
scores.M_why: KDP is flooded with AI-generated books. Amazon is tightening enforcement, discoverability is collapsing for low-content and AI titles, and readers can prompt the AI themselves.
scores.one_line: Nearly fully automatable with legal inbound, but the market is drowning in AI books and there are no first-hand earnings claims, so expect small, fragile royalties [E].

acquisition.why: The proven channels are door-knocking, local meetups and peer groups, which are human. Lawful agent-run cold email to limited companies and LinkedIn content are possible but conversion is unproven. Sole traders are off-limits for cold email.

onboarding.why: A voice-agent interview can run unattended with recording consent and a UK GDPR notice.

delivery.why: The transcript-to-report pipeline (Claude plus Gamma) is largely automated. The follow-up call and implementation upsells need Ricardo.

billing.why: Fixed-fee Stripe checkout. Implementation quotes need approval.

support.why: Presentation calls and implementation queries are human-heavy.

scores.R_why: Ricardo's technical skills fit and the setup cost is under £300. Converting UK SMEs to paid audits needs trust and calls that compete with 6-8 h/week. The upsell implementation is consulting time [E].
scores.M_why: An explosion of 'AI audit' agencies and freelancers, plus free self-serve AI assessment tools, means it is commoditising fast. A niche-vertical focus could help.
scores.one_line: The automated voice-interview-to-report pipeline is a neat agent fit, but selling it and the implementation upsell still lean on Ricardo's time in a crowded market [E].

acquisition.why: Podcast discovery comes through directories, YouTube clips, billboards and paid ads. Growth is slow and creative-led. The billboard example yielded about 30 downloads per episode.

onboarding.why: Listeners subscribe on platforms with no onboarding.

delivery.why: A host-led interview or history show needs Ricardo's voice, research judgement and guest booking. AI voice shows lack trust.

billing.why: Monetisation is unspecified. Dynamic ads and Patreon are automatic, but sponsorships need negotiation.

support.why: Minimal listener support; comments can be moderated by agents.

scores.R_why: Recording weekly episodes is feasible in 6-8 h/week, but monetisation is unstated and needs thousands of downloads per episode, which takes years for a new host [E].
scores.M_why: Podcasting is saturated, and AI-generated podcasts are flooding the field. Hits are concentrated among established hosts.
scores.one_line: A media hobby rather than a business model here: no revenue mechanism, host-dependent delivery and slow, expensive growth [E].
